title: Recognising immunotherapy-induced meningoencephalitis: a case during treatment for primary metastatic melanoma of the bladder neck
case_prompt:
A man in his 70s with a primary malignant melanoma of the bladder neck began combination ipilimumab and nivolumab 2 months after initial diagnosis. After his second infusion, he had increased fatigue and slept uninterrupted for 20 hours. Upon awakening, he stood up, fell, and was brought to the emergency department for confusion. His history included type 2 diabetes, but on admission he was not hypoglycaemic. Temperature was 37.8°C. On examination he was disoriented without focal neurologic deficits.  
Initial laboratory studies included a urine culture that grew Staphylococcus aureus, and intravenous antibiotics were started. Despite treatment, his mental status did not improve. A noncontrast CT scan of the head showed no acute intracranial pathology. Endocrine evaluation revealed hypopituitarism, and hormone replacement was initiated without neurologic improvement. He then developed no spontaneous speech, inappropriate responses, and apathy. Cerebrospinal fluid obtained via lumbar puncture showed lymphocytic pleocytosis; cultures, a viral panel, and separate HSV-1 and HSV-2 PCR tests were negative. MRI of the brain with and without contrast was limited by motion but showed bilateral basal ganglia hyperintensities on T2-weighted images and mild, inconclusive meningeal hyperintensities on FLAIR.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Hypoglycaemic event ruled out — “not hypoglycaemic on arrival, ruling out a hypoglycaemic event.”  
2. Urinary tract infection considered as a cause of confusion — “urine cultures came back positive for Staphylococcus aureus … but mental state continued to decline.”  
3. Stroke and metastatic intracranial pathology excluded by CT — “CT scan showed no evidence of acute intracranial pathology.”  
4. Hypopituitarism identified and treated without neurologic improvement — “Hypopituitarism, likely immune-related was noted and endocrinology advised on proper replacement therapy.”  
5. Infectious encephalitis excluded by CSF studies — “CSF cultures, viral panel and separate herpes simplex virus (HSV)-1 and HSV-2 CSF PCR tests were negative but CSF lymphocytosis was noted.”  
6. Toxic metabolic encephalopathy ruled out by blood workup — “Toxic metabolic causes were ruled out with blood workup that included chemistry comprehensive studies, basic haematology and thyroid studies.”  
7. Aseptic meningitis considered but deemed less likely given severe altered mental status — “altered mental status is less usual with aseptic meningitis.”
